title: Ripe for Revival debuts in Martin County - NewsBreak
text: Fridays may be the perfect day to do laundry while doing your grocery shopping. No, Walmart didn’t add a laundromat, but the Williamston Wash House is playing host to Ripe for Revival Mobile Market Program on Friday afternoons from 2 p.m. until 3:30 p.m. Ripe for Revival offers a mobile market complete with produce, frozen meats and other staples. Last Friday was the launch of the program in Martin County by the Rocky Mount organization, Ripe Revival. Ripe for Revival is the non-profit arm of the company simultaneously launched in Windsor last Thursday. “The launch in Bertie was very successful,” said Community Cultivation Coordinator Christine Marsh McKeel. McKeel began developing the Martin and Bertie county programs over a year ago and is excited about the dual launch. “We’ve been working on this for a long time. It’s great to be able to serve both communities. Yesterday was a terrific day in Bertie and so far today has been very busy,” said McKeel, referring to the 20 or so customers that had shown up by 2:30 p.m. While the mobile market was scheduled to be open at the Wash House last Friday, an accident in front of the location that afternoon forced the mobile market to park across the street. In the future it will be back at the Wash House. The Ripe for Revival Mobile Market Program was developed to bridge the gap between excess food and food insecurities due to a lack of access to healthy products. Food insecurities in Martin, Bertie and surrounding counties are staggering. In Martin County 32.4 percent of the population face food insecurities, in Bertie the number is higher at 32.6 percent of the population struggling with nutrition. Much of the problem is due to the high cost of groceries and a lack of places to purchase fresh produce. Ripe for Revival Mobile Market Program is attempting to alleviate some of the difficulties in finding healthy, reasonably priced foods. Will Kornegay is the founder and brainchild behind Ripe Revival. His passion for finding outlets for the produce grown by farmers and left to rot because of appearance and sell-ability led Kornegay into the food sector, creating outlets for the abundant produce. His success in that sector since 2020 led to the nonprofit development of Ripe for Revival Mobile Markets. Ripe For Revival’s Mobile Market Program takes the mission on the road by reconditioning large buses and box trailers into pay-what-you-can retail markets. The Mobile Markets provide fresh and local food to rural areas that tend to be “food deserts.” Ripe for Revival places a targeted focus on health and nutrition education. Walking into a Ripe for Revival Mobile Market is similar to walking into a small farm stand or farmers market. The walls are lined with shelves displaying boxes of peppers, bananas, lettuce, zucchini, yellow squash, onions, apples, potatoes and eggplant. Shoppers can also buy frozen meat and eggs. The Mobile Market is well stocked and the prices are cheaper than any store in the area. Plus, those who find it difficult to pay, can pay what they can. McKeel is busy cultivating communities. Currently, Ripe for Revival’s Mobile Market serves 20 counties and a growing number of families throughout eastern North Carolina. Ripe for Revival realizes it can’t solve food insecurities alone and believes in partnerships to help accomplish their goals. “We have a number of contributors who help us along the way. We have large donors, faith organizations, private companies and individuals. We also apply for grants. All of those partners help with funding,” said McKeel. “We could not do this without them. It makes such a difference on a community.” Subscribe to The Enterprise
